archetype.name: Pocket Passer (vertical)
archetype.definition: A non-running, rhythm-from-the-pocket passer whose value lives almost entirely in throws past 10 yards, with his legs contributing nothing and his feet in the pocket a liability once a rush gets home.

report.headline: Cleaner, more accurate passer, but blowout snaps flatter the efficiency
report.take:
Penix took the job in Week 3 after Cooper Rush and Tua Tagovailoa started the first two games, and he has been the best version of himself so far. The headline change is accuracy. His bad-throw rate has fallen from 22.5% last season to 10.4% (sixth-best of 38), and his CPOE has gone from -3.6 to slightly positive. That is not a small-sample wobble: in both 2024 and 2025 he ranked 51st in CPOE and near the bottom of the league in bad throws. The cause looks structural. He is getting the ball out faster (2.53 seconds, down from 2.79) and pushing it less often into tight windows, and the Falcons' line is keeping him cleaner than anyone's: pressured on 12.4% of dropbacks, the lowest rate among qualifiers.

What drives the production is the downfield game. Throws of 10+ air yards are worth 0.755 EPA a play and 34.0 EPA in total. Everything under 10 adds up to 5.9, dragged down by a screen and behind-the-line package that has cost 14.5 EPA. Drake London (0.715 EPA per target on 46 looks) and Kyle Pitts (0.702) are where the value goes. Bijan Robinson's targets are underwater. That gives him 8.81 adjusted net yards per dropback, fifth in the league, in an offense that runs more than its situations suggest (pass rate over expected ranks 27th).

The numbers hide two things. First, game script did a lot of the lifting. On 20 plays with a 9+ point lead he has 21.7 EPA, against a dropback total of 24.2. In one-score games he is at 0.032 EPA a play, essentially league-average. Those big-lead snaps came in the Green Bay and New Orleans blowouts. Second, when pressure does arrive he goes down: a 47.4% pressure-to-sack rate, worst of 38. Chicago got home and sacked him five times, he lost a fumble, and he posted -9.8 EPA even while throwing three touchdowns. He also has three fumbles charted as turnover-worthy against one interception.

The last three games are the more honest read. EPA per dropback is 0.065, still above the 0.04 league average but well off his season mark, and the sack rate is up to 7.5%. The Week 7 answer to San Francisco was telling: a 5.7-yard intended air distance, almost no aggressive throws, 25 of 34 and +5.5 CPOE. That is a quarterback the staff is protecting with timing throws, and it works when the line holds. The accuracy gains look real. The top-five efficiency built partly on two routs probably does not last.

strengths.title: Accuracy has genuinely changed
strengths.body: He has cut his bad-throw rate by more than half from last season and moved from a deeply negative CPOE to slightly positive. Both of his prior seasons sat near the bottom of the league in each, so this is a real shift, tied to a quicker release and fewer forced throws rather than luck. Expect most of it to hold, though tougher pass defenses will shave the edges.

strengths.title: Production lives past 10 yards
strengths.body: Intermediate and deep throws carry his EPA, with the 10+ group worth 34.0 against 5.9 underneath. London and Pitts turn those looks into points at roughly 0.7 EPA a target. The deep split is only 13 attempts, so its per-play figure will come down, but the intermediate game on 32 throws is the sturdier part.

strengths.title: Clean pockets and third-down poise
strengths.body: He faces pressure less than any qualifier, a product of a line that ranks third in limiting hits, and he has been sharp on third down at 0.46 EPA a play with a 44.4% conversion rate at 7.7 yards to go. The protection is a team trait more than his, so it moves with the line's health.

concerns.title: Pressure turns into sacks
concerns.body: When rushers get home, nearly half of those pressures end in sacks, the worst rate among qualifiers. This is not a scrambler's trade-off: four scrambles have gained 11 yards and no first downs. Chicago exposed it with five sacks and a lost fumble, and the recent sack rate has climbed. The low pressure rate masks the problem until a defense can win up front.

concerns.title: Efficiency inflated by blowouts
concerns.body: Twenty snaps with a big lead account for nearly all of his dropback EPA, while one-score situations sit near league average. Those leads came against Green Bay and New Orleans. In close games he has been ordinary rather than bad, and that is the level to expect against good defenses.

concerns.title: Touchdown and turnover luck
concerns.body: Seven red-zone touchdowns on 28 attempts with a 46.4% completion rate there is a hot rate, and a 0.7% interception rate sits far below his career norm of three picks in each partial season. Three turnover-worthy fumbles say the ball-security risk is already there. Expect the touchdown rate to cool and the giveaways to tick up.

trend.note: Four of his five starts landed between 7.6 and 10.6 passing EPA, with Chicago (-9.8) the outlier. Still, efficiency has slid since the blowout wins, and the Week 7 rebound came on a deliberately short, conservative plan.

nextGame.headline: Stingy Tampa pass defense, but its deep coverage leaks
nextGame.body:
Tampa Bay is the toughest pass defense he has seen: second in EPA allowed on passes, third on short throws, and the best in the league at holding opposing WR1s under their averages, a direct problem for a passer who leans on London. The opening is downfield. The Bucs rank only 17th against deep throws, and they don't generate much pressure (24th in hit rate), which plays to his clean-pocket comfort and hides his sack problem. A conservative, quick-game plan like the San Francisco approach will run into the Bucs' strength underneath, so the shots he takes past 10 yards decide the game.

Availability tilts slightly his way. Tampa is without safety Antoine Winfield Jr. (97% of snaps), which weakens the back end exactly where Penix does his damage. On offense the Bucs are missing WR Emeka Egbuka and tackle Luke Goedeke for an offense already 30th in passing EPA, which points to a lower-scoring, close game rather than a shootout. Atlanta is down WR Olamide Zaccheaus and RB Brian Robinson Jr., part-timers whose absence pushes more work to Jahan Dotson, Zachariah Branch and Bijan Robinson; the receiving-depth hit is minor. The forecast is early and shows a chance of thunderstorms, but the wind is modest, so it is not worth leaning on.

keyMatchups.title: London against a WR1 shutdown unit
keyMatchups.body: Tampa has held opposing top receivers further under their averages than any defense, and London is the engine of Penix's EPA. If London is muted, the passing game has to run through Pitts and Dotson, who have been far less efficient. Tampa is weaker against WR2s, which favors Dotson.

keyMatchups.title: Deep shots without Winfield
keyMatchups.body: The Bucs smother short throws but are middle-of-the-pack on deep passes, and they lose their best safety. Penix's best throws come beyond 10 yards, so this is where Atlanta should attack. Expect only a handful of attempts to swing his line.

keyMatchups.title: A rush that rarely gets home
keyMatchups.body: Tampa's hit rate ranks 24th, so the sack-prone pockets Chicago created are less likely here. With a backup tackle on Atlanta's IR, the line still has to hold, but this front isn't built to exploit his biggest flaw.

nextGame.watch: How many attempts he gets past 10 air yards: Tampa takes away the short game, so his ceiling depends on the staff letting him throw downfield at a secondary missing Winfield.

restOfSeason.body:
The accuracy and quicker release look like a real step forward, so a passer comfortably above league average per dropback is the baseline. The top-five adjusted yards figure will drift toward the 0.065 EPA-per-dropback level of his last three games, because big-lead snaps won't keep arriving. The offense runs more than it should, so volume stays moderate, around 29-33 attempts a game. That puts passing yards in a 205-250 range rather than a breakout pace.

The touchdown rate and the near-zero interception rate are the parts most likely to regress. Expect roughly 1.3 to 2.0 touchdowns a game, with occasional giveaways returning given the fumble history. He offers nothing as a runner, so his fantasy floor depends entirely on passing scores. His real swing variable is protection: as long as the line keeps pressure among the league's lowest, his sack problem stays contained.
swingFactors: Offensive line health and pressure rate
How often the staff lets him throw 10+ yards

confidence.note: Five starts, but the accuracy change is large and consistent; game-script inflation clouds the efficiency.
